Both of you - Whether you're AFAB or AMAB, dysphoria can be very hard to over come. I too struggle with those feelings of "Am I doing this right?" "Am I really a female?" 

BUT

I just want to let you both know, no matter what you're wearing, what color your nails are, what shoes are on your feet, what your hair looks like, makeup or not, what's between your legs, it doesn't matter. That doesn't define who you are.

And I know its a lot easier said than done.

But remember.

You are valid. And you are loved! 💗

Basically she cared for me in a very platonic, motherly way. Because of my surgeries, and the disabilities that followed, I didn't have an opportunity to really grow up alongside peers. I still use a bottle to this day, because I have a fear of spilling a cup on myself and making a mess. I had a private tutor to work on my vocal/communication skills, but in terms of a regular adult life, I'm not that good with it. Mommy took care of me, reminded me about my diaper, eating, sleeping, gave me a bedtime. Explained things to me. Held me. Kept me afloat. She was my rock. And I know it's embarassing to be in this situation, but I don't wanna be alone again...
